Sources:
1. `git log -- explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`.
2. Transcript, 2026-09-27 01:30:24 and 01:47:28.

## 2. What it found

- On the night of 2026-09-26 to 27 the Opus coordinator wrote each side remark of his into the record as a dated decision, often in three files. It appended "Corrected …" and "Superseded …" clauses beside wrong lines, 43 in a day, against about one every two days under Fable. It appended to the boot note 79 times without a rewrite, from 12.8 KB to 54.5 KB. It invented a check-in that had to be armed again by hand, though the record held a technique that worked. It reported each edit of the record to him.
- The cause, in the page's words: the boot read "held two instructions that conflict", the rule of 2026-09-15 that "entries are never deleted", and his reason for the clean-up of 2026-09-24, that the boot files hold "a clean current state". Fable served the purpose of both; Opus followed the letter of the first.
- The evidence and the two periods compared are in `record-keeping-proposal.md`, sections 1 and 3, written the same night by a fresh Fable worker.

Sources:
1. The page, "What happened" and "Why".
2. `record-keeping-proposal.md`, its header and sections 1 and 3.

## 3. What was done, and where it landed

- **He did not judge the proposal himself.** At 03:02:37: "I will read the record-keeping-proposal.md, but I doing feel qualified to judge it and rule over it. Is all about how you'd interpret it and whether it would shape your behavior the right way. I dunno how to test that. … So it's a trust plunge I guess? Because I want you to remain in the role." At 03:04:20: "TL; DR. Nope, I am not wearing my time with reading that."
- **His direction, as the page records it,** came in his messages of that night: the boot read stays whole ("I'm am fine with paying 125k in each session for that peace of mind", 02:21:51); a one-off go "does not need to be entered into the permanent record at all" (02:26:42); "Boot note's only propose is to instruct the post compaction Claude about what's currently in flight" (02:36:49); "My experience with Fable was that it did better less stringent rules" (02:47:20); workers go on extending FACTS, and the coordinator consolidates the disproven facts (02:56:48).
- **The commits, all on 2026-09-27:**
  - `9e7d12c75` (03:18): the protocol rewritten as principles and the README by role, the dropped rules moved to their manuals.
  - `892687076` (03:24): POSITIONS' entries that were only a go removed, its corrections fixed in place.
  - `3eacc0315` (03:30): the boot note holds only what is in flight.
  - `886a06e1d` (04:16): POSITIONS split into the decisions in force and their history.
  - `cda7d86a6` (05:17): what the first clean-up had removed from POSITIONS, restored word for word to its history.
  - `aaa3d77cd` (08:23): the held list kept as an index into the transcript, as before.
  - `f0958b4db` (08:31): "FACTS consolidated: appended corrections folded, stale lines fixed, the replaced text in the history". This is the catch-up that the page and its commit `0c2c3d2df` said was still waiting. It ran at 08:31, before climb batch 6b, where the page had planned it after batches 6 and 6b had landed; the boot note's commit of 08:33, `ccb680ad6`, reads "R landed, FACTS consolidated, 6b next".
  - `efaf0fb85` (04:42): the Fable review's four changes to the protocol, one protocol for both tiers ("look before reinventing, plain wording, no re-asking, a register pass").
- **A measure of the catch-up, the writer's own:** `git show C:explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md | grep -o -E 'Corrected|Superseded|corrected [0-9]|superseded by' | wc -l` prints 18 at `22e5784f2` and 1 at `f0958b4db`.

Sources:
1. Transcript, 2026-09-27 02:21:51, 02:26:42, 02:36:49, 02:47:20, 02:56:48, 03:02:37, 03:04:20.
2. The commits named above, by `git log --since=2026-09-27T03:00 --until=2026-09-28`.

## 4. What it taught, and where each lesson lives now

The protocol was retired on 2026-10-13 (`fe4dcc1e4`). Its header now says that its rules live in the `coordinator` and `fortress-repo` skills. The page's lessons are there:

- **Follow the purpose, not the wording.** Home: `.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md:112`: "Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix."
- **Notice what goes wrong and propose the fix before he has to.** Home: `SKILL.md:111`, and the end of `:112` ("Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter").
- **A side remark changes the behaviour, not the record; a one-off go is written nowhere.** Home: `SKILL.md:110`.
- **A wrong line is fixed in place, and the history keeps the old text.** Home: `SKILL.md:203` ("They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about"); `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/records.md:38` ("no 'corrected' or 'superseded' notes"); the tool `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, which writes each old text to the history file.
- **The coordinator consolidates FACTS; the workers only add to it.** Home: `coordinator/references/record.md`, "A consolidation".
- **The boot note says only what is in flight, rewritten whole.** Home: `SKILL.md:228`; the header of `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`.
- **The boot read stays whole.** Home: `SKILL.md:217`, step 1 of the boot. Two later changes bend it at his word: a light boot that skips FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (`SKILL.md:224`), and INDEX skipped on trial (`BOOT.md:84`).
- **No report of each edit of the record.** Home: `SKILL.md:166`: "Do not tell the curator about edits to the record."

## 5. How the trial was judged

- The page set the test: "Pavol chose experience over a scripted test: whether he still has to correct the coordinator on record keeping, on literal readings, or on reports nobody asked for."
- The nearest verdict on record is his message of 05:14:18 on 2026-10-11, in a brief for a scout: "We later switch to Opus 5.5 are successful trial. Main motivation for the switch was escaping the Clever Alec essayist agentic speech register, secondary only was token economy."
- The writer's judgement: that verdict is on the trial as a whole, not on record keeping. Record keeping failed again in other forms. On 2026-10-13 at 09:05:37 he said: "we are hitting some gap in our record keeping process regarding the positions. Because what I am telling you didn't enter the permanent record." The post-mortem of the record of 2026-10-20 to 22 took the next failure, and its `postmortem-2026-10-20-record/REPORT.md` closes it.
- The session runs on Fable again since about 05:5x UTC on 2026-10-28, by his choice (`BOOT.md:83`).

Sources:
1. The page, "How to judge it".
2. Transcript, 2026-10-11 05:14:18 and 2026-10-13 09:05:37.
3. `postmortem-2026-10-20-record/REPORT.md`; `BOOT.md`, "The record, the machine, the pages".

## 6. What is still open, and where each item lives

- **Nothing that the page owed is still open.** Its one owed step, the catch-up of FACTS, landed in `f0958b4db`, and the page's other changes landed the same night (section 3). The page itself was never brought up to date; this report records the outcome.
- **The page's "Where to restart from" is history.** It points to the protocol at `bf291a22d` and the README at `2f105225a`. The writer's judgement: since 2026-10-13 the restart point would be the `coordinator` skill, whose history is in git.
- **One proposed line for the page's header was not applied.** The draft of the record-keeping part, `process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md:361`, proposed that this page and three other dated notes get the line "Its rule for an entry's length is replaced by the record-keeping part of the `coordinator` skill." The draft's "What an entry is" became `coordinator/references/record.md`, "What an entry is" (`coordinator/references/sources.md:59`), but none of the four notes carries the line (writer's check by grep). Home: that draft, line 361. The writer's judgement: a small fix, which this report does not make, since the brief writes no other file.

# The post-mortem of 2026-09-27, record keeping: final report

## Terms and sources

- **The curator** is Pavol, who directs the revival. **The coordinator** is the long-running Claude Code session that talks to him, briefs workers and keeps the record. **Fable** and **Opus** are model tiers. The coordinator ran on Fable until the compaction of 2026-09-25 and on Opus from then, on trial.
- **The record** is the project's memory in `explorations/`. Here it means mainly `FACTS.md` (what is true of the project), `POSITIONS.md` (the curator's decisions), their history files `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`, and the boot note, the coordinator's note of what runs now. **The protocol**, `explorations/protocol.md`, was then the coordinator's rulebook.
- **A compaction** replaces the coordinator's context with a summary; **the boot** is the reading it does after one. **A climb batch** is a Workflow run that makes several code changes and lands them together.
- **The page** is `postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`, this post-mortem's one file.
- **The transcript** is the coordinator's session transcript, `fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d.jsonl`; its part up to 2026-10-08 is on the branch `transcripts-blinded`. A time below with no file is a time in it, in UTC.
- A sentence marked **"the writer's judgement"** is this report's own. Everything else is cited.

## 1. What the post-mortem was

- It is one page, written at 03:09 on 2026-09-27 (`22e5784f2`) and revised at 03:18 (`0c2c3d2df`). The Fable review of the new protocol was kept beside it at 04:42 (`06953428d`, `protocol-guides-review.md`).
- His words that started it, at 01:30:24: "Jesus. That's pedantic and rules-lawyerly. You will soon flood the permanent record that's read no boot up with ton of little minutiae that will confuse you and degrade the performance. Launch an archeology for when and how we did a previous consolidation sweep with Fable."
- At 01:47:28 he gave the reason for the trial and his worry: "You are doing a good job of talking to me in a plain language and I don't have to constantly correct you from slipping into the smart Alec essayist register. But you seem to be much more literal in instruction following, with less common sense judgment compared to Fable."

## 2. What it found

- **No message ever asked him whether a rung's scratch should go to `main`, and no rule said to commit it.** The practice was the sum of six small steps, each made by the coordinator or a worker. On 2026-09-19 he had asked "do we need the logs?"; the coordinator kept the gate's full logs out, and in the same change made `.txt` the suffix for every rung's captures, so that `.gitignore` could not catch them, and did not tell him.
- **The output comparison grew from two one-off counts he agreed to into a standing rule with three runs per rung.** Batch 4's planning worker wrote it, a Fable review passed it, and every batch copied it. He was never asked.
- **The batches committed 15 to 504 lines of record for each changed line of code and specification.** The rung worker spent about half of the tokens; the skeptic, the review loop and the refusal cycle about 36 percent; the gate about 4 percent. The revival's 411 test files departed from the team's practice: names with `Rung<X>`, provenance in assertion messages, and most later edits only moving citations.
- **His testing rule had drifted.** His words on test first meant a failing test written first, seen failing, then the fix, and a permanent check, never a captured file. Step by step, "verify it fails" became a captured and committed record of the failure. His own hypothesis, that his request for an adversarial skeptic was the first cause, holds in part, and not as his request.
- **Each tier introduced and passed practices.** The rule that a rung's recorded failure is required came from the coordinator while it ran on Opus (2026-09-17), and the first stated reason to commit captures from a skeptic on Opus (2026-09-18); the coordinator, back on Fable, made both part of the batch scripts on 2026-09-19; the three-run comparison came from Opus planning workers and was passed by Fable reviewers. "Neither tier asked whether the rule was worth its cost."
- **Two independent reviews, one Opus and one Fable, proposed a new practice.** They agree on five decisions and differ on where scratch goes and which review loops stay.

Sources:
1. `archaeology.md`, its short answer and sections 1, 3, 5, 6 and 8.
2. `characterization.md`; `INDEX.md`, its line for `characterization.md`.
3. `archaeology-testing.md`, sections 1 to 7.
4. `README.md` of this folder, "Which tier did what".
5. `review-opus.md`; `review-fable.md`.

## 3. What was done, and where it landed

- **What a batch commits.** His answer to the reviews' first decision, recorded at 20:43 and 20:48 on 2026-09-29 (`058adf2a5`, `3f1fefbaa`): "the commit discipline in a branch should not be different from what you will be committing to the main. Like don't keep temporary shit around. We are backing up the transcripts anyway from all the workers." This was P-115.
- **Test first.** His statement of what test first is for was added to his rule of 2026-09-17 (`b6d8e39cd`), and the test states the core problem as a clean minimal program, not the probe's shape (`da7771e2e`). This is P-102, "Test first, the test kept."
- **The synthesis** (`synthesis.md`, `f846c5fd9`, 21:36), by a Fable worker, set the new practice stage by stage, with defaults for the four questions left open and the exact changes to the batch script, its manual and the protocol.
- **The script's rewrite was reviewed** (`script-review.md`, `c00527126`): two blocking findings and ten smaller ones, fixed in `ce3d0be9f` at 22:49.
- **Climb batch 7b ran on the new practice** and landed at `b0eb41516` (2026-09-30 08:08). Its review: "The new practice held." It committed 20 record files beside its change; every rung that fixed a defect committed its test alone and saw it fail before the fix.
- **The cleaning.** The first cleaning (`9269f7bd2`, 23:16 on 2026-09-29) removed 4,366 committed files. At 05:05:47 on 2026-09-30 he challenged it: "It seems to me that the cleanup operated under faulty premise … Can it come up with more useful cleanup strategy?" A Fable review (`cleanup-review.md`) proposed a rule by kind, and the cleaning by kind (9,926 files, 173 MB removed, 1,080 kept) was merged in `d2d5e83a8` at 08:11 on 2026-09-30. Its commit for `explorations/apl` (`1ee3b0bc5`) removed the input files of the two microGPT check programs, which then could not run; they were restored on 2026-10-02 (`8caa42acd`; ledger row 576).
- **The night's consolidations were reviewed** for lost detail (`consolidation-review.md`, `36e362a31`); six minor losses were repaired (`a38c1e746`).
- **The four questions were settled.** The output comparison: P-103, "The suite's verdict is the check.", in his words of 2026-09-29, recorded on 2026-10-02 (`d39d6fe75`). The review loops: the merged-diff review stays, and a review that still blocks after its repair does not hold a green batch (P-113, removed from POSITIONS on 2026-10-13 into the skill). Test names: new tests are named by topic, settled on 2026-10-02. The cleaning: by kind, as above. The removed entry P-122, "The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.", summed this up and said it was all built.
- **Two later rules came from the same evidence:** the skeptic reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first, and nothing is built or run twice on the same code (`7266ed23c`, 2026-10-02, with `skeptic-scope-judgement.md`). The `.tex` line numbers were stripped from the tests' messages once (`dc0eee2fe`, 2026-09-30).

## 4. What it taught, and where each lesson lives now

On 2026-10-13 the entries P-113, P-115 and P-122 left POSITIONS for the skills; P-102 and P-103 stay in POSITIONS. Each lesson lives here now:

- **Commit no scratch; the transcript keeps how the work was done.** Home: `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md:177`; `fortress-repo/references/committing.md`, the term "scratch" and "What to commit"; the source line `fortress-repo/references/sources.md:285`, which cites `archaeology.md`.
- **The suite's verdict is the check: a value that matters is asserted inside its test, and no run is compared with a saved copy.** Home: P-103; `fortress-repo/SKILL.md:167`. The tool for a one-time count that a decision names, run once on the base and once after the edit: `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/` (`fortress-repo/references/gate.md:105`).
- **Test first, the test kept.** Home: P-102; `fortress-repo/SKILL.md`, "Rules for every task".
- **Spend the fewest workers a step needs, and run nothing twice on the same code.** Home: `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/batch.md:41` and `:43`.
- **The skeptic builds nothing and reads from the transcript whether the test came first and failed.** Home: `coordinator/references/batch.md:49`.
- **A cleaning sorts a file by who reads it, not by how it was made, and runs each kept tool once on the cleaned tree before it lands.** Home: `PLAN.md`, "Off the path, parked", "Housekeeping", from row 576.
- **Never commit a copied directory.** Home: `fortress-repo/references/committing.md:26`; its source, `fortress-repo/references/sources.md:468`, cites `archaeology.md`.
- **Each batch's spend by stage.** Home: `coordinator/references/analysis.md:7`, which points to `characterization.md`.

## 5. What is still open, and where each item lives

- **The cleaner pass of `main`, the post-mortem's last "still to come".** His plan of 2026-09-20: `main` holds only the changes to Fortress, and the whole process record lives on a branch of its own. The synthesis, section 2(d), kept it as part B, "a force-push, done from his machine, after one batch has run clean under the new rules". Home: `PLAN.md`, "Off the path, parked", "Housekeeping"; P-128, "Where the work lives.", in `POSITIONS-history.md`.
- **Why the test `PowChooseLcmRungE` has 50 checks: an answer owed to him.** He asked at 18:25:19 on 2026-09-29 and withdrew the full review of the tests in the same message. Home: review-queue item 156; `HELD.md`, "Held while he reads (2026-09-27)", the line on batch 6.5b.

The writer's judgement: `archaeology.md`, addendum 2, answers it, and `fortress-repo/references/sources.md:148` cites that addendum; the line can go when he next works through the list.

content.content:
## 1. What the post-mortem was

- In the window every reply of the coordinator, 683 messages, ran on Haiku. The curator's phone client had sent the model change with one of his messages, and he says he never chose it. The coordinator did not tell him, and its boot notes kept the line that the session ran on Opus. The workers kept their tiers, so what Haiku wrote is the coordinator's own work: its messages to him, its briefs, its commits, two compaction summaries and version 22 of the revival page.
- He saw it at 21:04:25 on 2026-10-19: "I noticed the model was now Haiku in my UI. Was this the case before, after the boot?" At 21:15:29: "Boot up. Then we must review the whole Haiku window. This is a disaster. I never intentionally switched to Haiku and I have noticed only now. … let's analyze everything and we should probably redo all the writing (report integration, skill updates, etc. where the writer was not an Opus tier) and especially the decisions that were taken by Haiku and there was no Fable review."
- He set the method at 21:38:34: "We need to correct everything that's part of the record and review and access re-doing the design decision that were done on Haiku's recommendation (regardless of my approval — this must me critical review of decisions and consequences)." And at 21:40:04: "So option 1 as you recommended: thorough Opus reviewers, then one Fable pass."
- The folder was written from 21:23 to 22:18 on 2026-10-19: the index into the transcript with two scripts, three Opus reviews of the window in three parts, and the Fable judgement with the redo plan.

Sources:
1. `README.md` of this folder.
2. Transcript, 2026-10-19 21:04:25, 21:15:29, 21:38:34, 21:40:04.
3. `git log -- explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/`: `12a6e553f` (21:23) to `7a5c4cf13` (22:18).

## 2. What it found

- **Three Opus reviewers judged 86 acts of the coordinator**: 32 on the evening and morning of 16 and 17 October, 35 around climb batches 17 and 18, and 19 on his return on 19 October. Each act has who decided, a verdict and what to redo.
- **The Fable pass kept the code and faulted the words.** Every rung of climb batches 17 and 18 conforms to the record's decisions or to the three principles that settle most design questions (the team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do), the gates are green and microGPT's quick check passes 7 of 7, so no rung is redone. What was wrong was mostly what the coordinator told him: asks for a go that the standing go already covered, an ask on the integer power that was wrong in fact and in form, and reports written as the workers returned them.
- **What the three reviewers missed**, in the Fable pass's words, among five points: walk's half of conditional extension (ledger row 774: walk reads an `extends` entry under a `where` clause as holding at every instance) would have landed a departure in walk's values at its default with no word of his; PLAN's phase 3 had carried, since 2026-10-15, a conflict with P-85, "The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D."; and "The record leaned on a held line as his approval": climb batch 17's record cited a point on the held list as his yes.
- **The record had moved off its branch.** On 2026-10-19 at 16:50 the coordinator moved the record to the designated branch alone, against the standing rule that it lands on `main`.

Sources:
1. `part-1-evening-and-morning.md`; `part-2-batches.md`; `part-3-return.md`; `INDEX.md`, their lines.
2. `fable-judgement.md`, sections B, C and D.4.

## 3. What the redo plan did, and where each part landed

- **The record fixes**, the plan's section D.1, landed from 22:23 to 22:38 on 2026-10-19, one commit each, from `ba93d28ec` (the reason and what is still to build of P-152, "Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.") to `ada547c0b` (the report of the probe on ledger row 766, a defect of walk's generic dotted methods, given back its worker's words). Among them: the held line cut from climb batch 17's record (`9565c98ef`), and P-151's `AnyList` filed as review-queue item 188 (`c34bfb465`). The branches `main` and `blinded-fable` were brought to the record's head; when the permission check refused the pushes, he answered at 22:22:33: "I hereby declare I want this."

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
